\subsection{Deterministic chores}
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:deterministic-chores}
For $n\ge3$ finite nonnegative nonatomic chore costs, a deterministic
Eval/Cut protocol returns a complete exactly envy-free allocation using
\[
 Q,C\le 2^{3n\log_2 n+O(n)}.
\]
The guarantee holds for every legal Cut response. The one- and two-agent
cases have constant-size protocols.
\end{theorem}
Appendix~\ref{r8c:appendix} gives the construction and the explicit bound
$2^{14n(\lceil\log_2n\rceil+1)}$. The main improvement comes from pooling
compensation tasks and bounding the number of times the pool must shrink.
A $2^{O(n)}$ bound, and in particular the $n^{O(1)}2^n$ bound known for cake,
remain open for chores.

\subsection{Randomized cake and chores}
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:general-upper}
For every profile of $n$ finite nonnegative nonatomic measures, interpreted
as cake values or as chore costs, a Las Vegas Eval/Cut protocol returns a
complete exactly envy-free allocation with
\[
 \E{Q}=O(n^{21}\log^2(2n)),\qquad
 \E{C}=O(n^{20}\log^2(2n)).
\]
The protocol uses exact real arithmetic and independent uniform-real
samples. The bounds hold uniformly over profiles and legal measurable
nonanticipating Cut policies, including all rejected work.
\end{theorem}
Here nonanticipating means that a reply may depend on the past and the
current query, but not on future random choices. The full proof is in
Appendix~\ref{r6u:appendix}. For cake, the result improves a known polynomial
expected-query bound. The same construction supplies a polynomial
expected-query bound for chores.

\subsection{A randomized lower bound}
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:nonnegative-lower}
Fix $p\in(0,1]$. Suppose a measurable randomized interval-query protocol
returns a complete exactly envy-free allocation with probability at least
$p$ on every normalized finite-step cake profile, or on every such chore
profile, whose densities lie in $[1/2,3/2]$. Then, for all sufficiently
large $n$, its unconditional expected query count on the uniform profile is
\[
 \E{Q_{\mathrm{unif}}}=\Omega_p(n^2).
\]
The protocol may use ideal-real randomness and return allocations with
arbitrarily many intervals, choosing their endpoints without oracle calls.
\end{theorem}
The subscript $p$ permits the constant to depend on the fixed success
probability. The protocol must work on the entire stated class, although
the expected cost is charged on the uniform input. Appendix~\ref{r6lb:appendix}
proves the explicit bound $n(np-1)^2/[2(n-1)]$ whenever
$np\ge3-2/n$, including unsuccessful outcomes. Thus the result strengthens
the randomness and success guarantees covered by a quadratic lower bound;
it does not raise its asymptotic order.

\subsection{Mixed cake and chores}
For signed valuations, define \emph{$\alpha$-multiplicative envy-freeness},
where $0<\alpha\le1$, by the relative-envy condition
\begin{equation}\label{eq:signed-relative-ef}
 v_i(A_j)-v_i(A_i)
 \le (1-\alpha)\max\{|v_i(A_i)|,|v_i(A_j)|\}
 \qquad(i,j\in[n]).
\end{equation}
This definition handles either sign and zero values without dividing by a
net total. For nonnegative cake values it is the usual guarantee
$v_i(A_i)\ge\alpha v_i(A_j)$~\cite{BK23}; for nonnegative chore costs it
is $c_i(A_i)\le c_i(A_j)/\alpha$. At $\alpha=1$ it is exact EF.
Our hard instances have total value one for every agent. Any allocation
satisfying the relative guarantee then gives each agent positive own value,
so the condition is equivalent to the usual cake inequality.
Lemma~\ref{r6m:relative-equivalence} gives the proof. Hardness on this
subclass suffices for the general signed domain.

We state additive approximation separately. On profiles normalized by
$v_i(I)=1$, additive $\eps$-envy-freeness means
$v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j)-\eps$. This tolerance is in net-value units.
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:mixed-mc}
Fix $n\ge3$, a success probability $p\in(0,1]$, and a multiplicative factor
$\alpha\in(0,1]$. For finite signed nonatomic measures,
no measurable randomized protocol can guarantee both
$\alpha$-multiplicative envy-freeness with probability at least $p$ on
every input and a uniform finite expected-query bound. This already holds
when $v_i(I)=1$ for every agent. On that normalized subclass, the same
conclusion holds for additive $\eps$-envy-freeness for every fixed
$0\le\eps<1$.

The oracle uses signed bracketed Eval/Cut queries. The impossibility
holds even when Cut must return the rightmost root if the bracket total
is nonnegative, and the leftmost root otherwise. It also holds with
these two choices reversed. No common total-variation ceiling is imposed. Ideal-real randomness is allowed, and output cut
locations may be chosen without queries, with no bound on their number.
\end{theorem}
The theorem concerns the information needed to find an allocation.
It does not rule out existence, bound the minimum number of output cuts,
or require a single input to have infinite expected cost. It already
holds for finite piecewise-constant densities. Appendix~\ref{r6m:appendix}
proves both approximation statements together through the inequality
$\alpha v_i(A_j)-v_i(A_i)\le\eps$, for $0\le\eps<\alpha\le1$.
The absence of a common variation ceiling allows increasingly large
positive and negative masses to cancel while every net total stays one.
The two root rules depend on the sign of the bracket total. The result
does not address an oracle that always returns the leftmost root or
always returns the rightmost root, nor a class with a fixed common
bound on total variation.
